title: Writing Your First Go Program
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and behavior of writing your first go program.
Apply at least one lesson concept—printing hello, world—in a small Go example or workflow.
Predict a representative result, then test a boundary case and explain any difference.

content.intro: Writing Your First Go Program is part of the foundation for using Go reliably. Start by identifying the goal, checking the toolchain or runtime assumptions, and reproducing the result with the documented Go commands. Do not assume that a command or setting is identical on every operating system.
content.why_it_matters: You need this topic to set up a repeatable workflow and distinguish an installation/configuration problem from a language or application defect.

content_blocks.title: Walk through the example
content_blocks.text: First, identify the input or initial state in the example for writing your first go program. Next, trace the operation or contract that matters, and predict the result before running it. If the example depends on a version-specific feature, a driver, or an external service, follow the stated prerequisites rather than assuming it works in a browser preview.

content.task: Create a small example connected to “Writing Your First Go Program”. Use Printing Hello, World as the starting point, predict the output, then add one invalid, empty, or boundary case and document its result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates printing hello, world or a closely related concept.
Inputs, relevant state changes, and expected output are clear.
At least one boundary case is deliberately tested or documented.
Errors are handled honestly and no success state is reported when the operation fails.
hints: Start from the simplest example related to printing hello, world.
Predict the result manually and annotate the value that changes at each step.
Run `gofmt` and the appropriate local `go run`, `go test`, `go vet`, or inspection command when prerequisites are available.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the happy-path output proves all inputs are safe.
common_mistakes.why: Empty, malformed, boundary, or concurrent cases may follow different paths.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused tests for a normal input and at least one relevant edge case.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring returned errors or external-system status.
common_mistakes.why: Go APIs commonly report expected failures as explicit error values.
common_mistakes.fix: Check errors close to the operation, add useful context when propagating, and clean up resources.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an API or syntax without checking the selected Go version.
common_mistakes.why: Language and standard-library capabilities can change between releases.
common_mistakes.fix: Record `go version`, inspect the `go` directive, and read official release notes for version-specific topics.

summary: Writing Your First Go Program provides a reusable rule or workflow for Go programs.
The subtopics to revisit are: Printing Hello, World; Understanding the main package; Understanding func main(); Running a source file; Building a standalone executable.
Prefer a small reproducible example, explicit errors, appropriate tests, and version-matched official documentation.
